newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat may get less land than he bargained for.
newsitem.headline: Arafat may get less land than he bargained for.

text.p: With the smoke from the battle for Hebron barely cleared, Israeli and Palestinian negotiators are girding for a bloodier political war over the rest of the West Bank.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat got 80 percent of Hebron and thinks he will control an even higher proportion of the West Bank once Israel completes a three-stage handover next year.
But the self-rule agreements he signed with the ousted Labour government do not say how far Israeli troops are to withdraw.

The point is not lost on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu who is trying to hold together a right-wing coalition government and a country that are split over handing back Palestinian land captured in the 1967 Middle East War.

"It is not true, contrary to what you have been told, that the so-called redeployments in the interim agreement bring us to the '67 boundaries, or 80 percent or 90 percent of it," Netanyahu told U.S. rabbis this week.

"It doesn't stipulate any percentage. It doesn't stipulate any territory," Netanyahu said, signalling that Palestinians are in for some tough bargaining if they are to govern more than the main towns and villages.
"Our purpose is to stay not to leave," Netanyahu said.
PLO and Labour government officials negotiated the two Oslo self-rule agreements from 1993 to 1995 in an atmosphere of trust that vanished after Netanyahu's election in May.
They deliberately kept figures out of the text but PLO officials say they understood from their contacts with the Israelis that they would control 90 percent of the West Bank.
"We did not specify the area of the West Bank and Gaza Strip in the 1995 interim deal but we are confident about our percentages," PLO official Ahmed Korei told Reuters.

"We believe that after the third phase of redeployments is completed, 87 to 90 percent of the West Bank and Gaza Strip would be under our jurisdiction," he said. "If the Israelis are giving different percentages, then they are trying to change the agreement and are trying to swallow our land."
Yossi Beilin, a Labour minister who helped negotiate Oslo, said the scale of the Israeli withdrawal was always open to debate.

"The final stage is up to the negotiators," he told Reuters. He said the last of the three redeployments was supposed to be linked to negotiations on a final settlement of the Israeli- Palestinian conflict, scheduled to be in place by May 4, 1999.

Israeli analysts think Arafat might end up with only half of the West Bank with Israel retaining control of the 140 Jewish settlements, military locations and borders. This would be similar to the deal on Gaza where Israel still has about 40 percent of the Strip.

"It's hard to imagine Palestinians are going to get 90 percent," said Mark Heller of the Jaffee Centre for Strategic Studies. "Because if that's the case there's nothing left to talk about," he said, referring to the "final status" negotiations which are due to determine the shape of Palestinian autonomy, tackling such thorny issues as borders, Jerusalem and refugees.

Israeli analysts believe the first two withdrawals after Hebron will be determined solely by Israel and will be small. Israel will insist the third redeployment reflect a negotiated understanding on the scope of Palestinian autonomy.
Palestinains think differently.

"The agreement is clear, it states that redeployment from the rest of the West Bank should be parallel to final status talks, which means that most of the land would be under our control before we end those talks," Korei, better known as Abu Alaa, said.

"Final status issues are Jerusalem which is less than one percent (of the land area), settlements around seven percent, borders less than one percent and military locations around two percent," he said.
Not so, argue the Israelis, unwilling to lose leverage in the final status talks. They say that the Oslo accords stipulate Israel will redeploy to "specified military locations".
"It says military locations not bases," notes Heller. "Most of the Jordan Valley and Judean desert could be considered military locations," he said.
"It seems there are some potential timebombs in the Olso agreements that were overlooked."
